title: Preanalytic Errors, Order of Draw, Specimen Rejection, POCT, and Laboratory Mathematics
summary: The error phase nobody sees on the analyzer: patient preparation, tube order of draw and additive carryover, hemolysis, icterus, and lipemia, transport and storage, objective specimen rejection criteria, point-of-care testing governance, and the arithmetic every bench relies on - dilutions, C1V1=C2V2, unit conversions, and titer logic.
objectives: List the major preanalytic error sources and their effects on common chemistry and hematology results.
State the standard order of draw and explain the rationale (additive carryover) behind it.
Apply objective specimen rejection criteria and communicate with wards without shaming staff.
Perform basic laboratory calculations: dilutions, C1V1=C2V2, unit conversions, and simple quality-control math.

highYield: Order of draw (CLSI-aligned practice): blood culture bottles, citrate (light blue), serum (red/tiger), heparin (green), EDTA (lavender), glycolytic inhibitor (gray).

Hemolysis falsely elevates potassium, LDH, AST, magnesium, and phosphate and can falsely lower analytes measured by methods affected by hemoglobin absorbance; it is the single most common cause of specimen rejection.

Citrate tubes must be filled to within the manufacturer's stated range (commonly 90 to 110 percent of nominal fill) because underfilling raises the citrate-to-blood ratio and prolongs coagulation times.
Every specimen needs at least two patient identifiers before acceptance; mislabeled specimens are rejected regardless of quality.
C1V1 = C2V2: what goes in equals what comes out - the backbone of every dilution calculation.

quickReview.mnemonic: Order of draw: 'Boys Can Really Have Easy Girls' - Blood cultures, Citrate, Red, Heparin, EDTA, Gray (glycolytic inhibitor).

deepStudy.introduction: Most laboratory errors happen before the specimen reaches the analyzer - wrong patient, wrong tube, wrong fill, wrong temperature, wrong timing - and the preanalytic phase is where the laboratory professional's judgment matters most because no instrument flags a mislabeled tube. This lesson covers the practical prevention system: patient preparation, order of draw and additive carryover, specimen integrity markers (hemolysis, icterus, lipemia indices), transport and storage rules, and transparent specimen rejection criteria that protect patients without blaming nurses or phlebotomists. Alongside runs the mathematics of the bench: dilutions, concentration-volume algebra, unit conversions, and titers, which must be exact because a decimal-point slip changes a patient's dose or a blood bank's decision. Point-of-care testing ties it together because operators outside the laboratory perform patient-side testing under the laboratory's quality umbrella. All numeric cutoffs quoted here (fill ranges, storage temperatures, conversion factors) reflect widely published teaching values; laboratories must verify them against their own validated procedures and local policies before implementation.

sections.heading: Patient preparation and specimen integrity
sections.body: Preanalytic variables begin with the patient: fasting status affects glucose and triglycerides; posture and tourniquet time hemoconcentrate proteins and lipids; recent exercise raises potassium, CK, and myoglobin; hemolysis during collection (small needle, traumatic draw, aggressive syringe aspiration) releases potassium, LDH, AST, and phosphate from red cells and interferes with colorimetric methods. Icterus (bilirubin) and lipemia (triglycerides) are the other two classic interferents; modern analyzers flag all three with serum indices (hemolysis, icterus, lipemia - HIL) so the laboratory can comment rather than guess. Diet and drugs matter too: biotin interferes with streptavidin-biotin immunoassays, and high-dose vitamin C alters colorimetric and dipstick chemistry. Timing governs therapeutic drug monitoring (draw at the right interval from dose), cardiac markers (serial draws on a defined clock), and blood cultures (before antibiotics whenever possible). Specimen acceptance begins with matching at least two patient identifiers to the requisition; identity errors are catastrophic and non-negotiable - the tube is rejected and recollected. The laboratory's job is to document preparation status (fasting, posture, time of draw) when it changes interpretation and to communicate patterns - repeated hemolysis from one ward, say - as system feedback rather than individual blame.

sections.heading: Order of draw: why sequence matters
sections.body: The order of draw exists because trace additive carryover from one tube contaminates the next. The widely taught CLSI-aligned sequence for venipuncture is: blood culture bottles first (their broth needs undiluted blood and sodium polyanethol sulfonate), then light blue sodium citrate coagulation tubes, then serum tubes (red, tiger/clot activator or gel), then green heparin tubes, then lavender EDTA tubes, and finally gray fluoride/oxalate tubes for glycolysis inhibition. The classic contamination example is EDTA carryover into a citrate tube: excess EDTA binds calcium and falsely prolongs PT and aPTT; conversely, citrate carryover into a potassium sample falsely lowers potassium. Underfilled citrate tubes raise the citrate-to-blood ratio and prolong clotting times - coagulation tubes must be filled to the manufacturer's stated range (commonly near 90 to 110 percent of nominal volume) and underfilled tubes outside that range are rejected per protocol. Multiple-additive tubes can change the sequence when a single draw handles several tests; when in doubt, follow your laboratory's validated procedure and the tube manufacturer's instructions, because local policy resolves edge cases. Butterfly needle draws may require a discard tube before a citrate tube to fill the dead space; again, follow local procedure. The exam version is short: cultures, citrate, serum, heparin, EDTA, gray - and the reason is additive carryover, not superstition.

sections.heading: Specimen rejection: criteria that hold up
sections.body: Objective rejection criteria protect patients from results that look precise but are wrong. Universally rejected: specimens without two patient identifiers or with mismatched identifiers (never relabel a mislabeled tube - recollect), unlabeled or improperly labeled tubes, leaked or broken containers, and specimens unsuitable for the test ordered (wrong tube type, clotted EDTA whole blood for CBC, clotted citrate). Conditionally rejected with clinician consultation when possible: hemolyzed specimens (hemolysis index exceeding the analyzer or method's validated limit for the affected analytes), insufficient volume (especially citrate underfill), transport outside validated temperature or time windows, QNS (quantity not sufficient) volumes, and specimens drawn from lines with infusion contamination (for example, glucose-containing IV fluids). Coagulation specimens with clots or underfill are rejected; body fluids and urine for culture transported at room temperature for extended periods may be rejected or commented. Documentation records who was notified, when, and the disposition (recollect versus proceed with comment). Communication tone matters: rejection is a quality function, not a reprimand; patterns go to committees as system problems (procurement of difficult tubes, staffing at draw times), while single events get a call and a recollect. A rejection policy without documentation is a policy that will fail inspection and, worse, fail the patient whose bad number quietly slipped through.

sections.heading: Point-of-care testing: laboratory oversight at the bedside
sections.body: Point-of-care testing moves methods out of the laboratory but not out of laboratory governance. Glucose meters, blood gas analyzers, rapid strep and influenza assays, urinalysis readers, and activated clotting time devices are operated by nurses, respiratory therapists, or physicians under a quality system the laboratory director oversees: operator training and competency assessment (initial and periodic, typically every 6 to 12 months per policy), documented QC with electronic lockout where available, consumable lot tracking, instrument maintenance logs, and result review in the clinical record. CLIA-waived status simplifies the regulatory floor but never waives the manufacturer's instructions; moderate-complexity POC devices carry full nonwaived obligations including proficiency testing where applicable. Glucose meters deserve special caution: results differ between capillary and venous samples, and hematocrit extremes, oxygen tension, perfusion, and interfering substances (for example, maltose in some peritoneal dialysis solutions, uric acid, acetaminophen at high levels on some chemistries) bias readings; meters read whole blood but report plasma-equivalent values on most current systems. Critical results at POC must have defined alert limits and callback pathways identical in seriousness to central laboratory critical values. The recurring principle: decentralization of instruments does not decentralize accountability.

sections.heading: Laboratory mathematics: the arithmetic of the bench
sections.body: Bench math is small, exact, and consequential. Dilutions express part over whole: a 1:5 dilution is one part sample plus four parts diluent; serial dilutions multiply factors, so three 1:10 steps give 1:1,000. The dilution equation C1V1 = C2V2 states that concentration times volume is conserved: to make 50 mL of working solution at 2 mol/L from 10 mol/L stock, V1 = (2 x 50) / 10 = 10 mL stock plus 40 mL diluent. Unit conversions ride on molar mass and standard factors: glucose mg/dL multiplied by 0.0555 gives mmol/L, BUN mg/dL multiplied by 0.357 gives mmol/L urea, and creatinine mg/dL multiplied by 88.4 gives micromoles per liter. Osmolality and anion-gap style calculations are covered in the formulas sheet. Dilutions for cell counts use the same logic: 20 microliters of blood in 1.98 mL diluent is a 1:100 dilution, multiplied by chamber volume and grid factor to give cells per liter. Percent solutions: 0.9 percent NaCl is 0.9 g per 100 mL. Titer arithmetic reports the reciprocal of the last positive dilution. Accuracy checks: an answer that is orders of magnitude away from expected physiology is usually a unit slip, not a patient event - estimate before you calculate, and verify decimal placement twice for anything that changes therapy or transfusion. Show your work on worksheets; inspections and incident reviews both ask how the number was derived.

deepStudy.clinicalSignificance: Preanalytic discipline prevents misdiagnosis at the source: a hemolyzed potassium triggers cardiac workups, an underfilled citrate tube diagnoses coagulopathy that does not exist, and a mislabeled tube can transfuse the wrong blood. Specimen rejection protocols cut repeat testing, antibiotic courses on contaminated cultures, and length of stay. POCT glucose accuracy drives insulin dosing at the bedside; a biased meter is a patient safety event. Laboratory mathematics underpins dilutions for blood bank titers, therapeutic drug dosing calculations, and QC remediation. In short, the preanalytic phase is where most preventable patient harm in laboratory medicine lives, and it is the phase laboratory professionals own.
deepStudy.labInterpretation: Report HIL indices with comments (for example, hemolyzed specimen - potassium, LDH, AST, phosphate unreliable) rather than silently releasing values. For coagulation, state fill adequacy and reject clotted or underfilled citrate tubes per procedure. For POC, report results with operator, device, and time, and route them to the clinical record through the same interface as central laboratory results. For all calculations, retain worksheet documentation showing the equation, values, units, and the final result with its significant figures. Whenever a numeric threshold (fill range, storage temperature, conversion factor) is applied, cite the source procedure; never quote cutoffs from memory in reports - the laboratory's validated values govern, and intervals vary by laboratory, method, and population.

examTraps: Order of draw is about additive carryover, not convenience; EDTA carryover into citrate falsely prolongs coagulation tests while citrate carryover falsely lowers potassium.
Never relabel a mislabeled specimen - the tube is rejected and the patient redrawn; relabeling destroys the only evidence of the identity error.
Fluoride slows glycolysis but does not stop it immediately; glucose specimens still need prompt separation or validated transport conditions.
A 1:10 dilution means one part sample in ten parts total (nine parts diluent), not one part sample plus ten parts diluent.
deepStudy.workedExample:
**Dilution worksheet**

A urine culture needs a 1:100 and a 1:1,000 dilution plated at 0.01 mL each. For 1:100: 0.1 mL urine into 9.9 mL saline (total 10 mL). For 1:1,000: take 1 mL of the 1:100 tube into 9 mL saline (a further 1:10 step, cumulative 1:1,000). If the 1:100 plate grows 45 colonies and the plated volume is 0.01 mL, the original concentration is 45 / 0.01 / 100 = 45,000 CFU/mL after applying the dilution factor - and the 1:1,000 plate should grow about 4 to 5 colonies, which is exactly the consistency check that catches decimal errors before reporting.
